fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot of truth to it, though I'd put it a bit more carefully. I don't think most components are random. Each one was introduced for a good reason at the time it appeared. The issue is that the reason often belongs to a specific moment, and the component outlives the moment.

Normalization is my favorite example. Batch norm showed up around 2015 because people were trying to train deeper networks with the optimizers and initialization schemes they had then. It worked, so everyone kept it. Then layer norm came in with Transformers, and now it's just assumed that you need a normalization layer in every block. But if you actually go back and ask what the layer is doing in a trained model, you find it mostly acts like a squashing function on the extreme values. That was what motivated our work on replacing it with a simple element-wise tanh. The network trains fine without any normalization at all. Nobody tried hard, because the default was already good enough.

The ConvNeXt project taught me the same lesson from a different angle. When Vision Transformers started winning, the narrative was that attention was the key ingredient. But when we took a standard ResNet and ported over the design decisions that came with Transformers, things like the training recipe, the patchify stem, larger kernels, fewer activations, fewer normalization layers, the inverted bottleneck, the ConvNet caught up. A lot of what looked like architectural superiority turned out to be a bundle of choices that happened to be made together when a new architecture arrived.

So my view is that architectures evolve more like biology than like engineering. Something gets fixed in place because it worked under the conditions of the time, and then everything downstream adapts to it, so it becomes expensive to remove even when the original reason is gone. The compute budgets, the data scales, and the optimizers today are completely different from 2015. It would be strange if every default from that era were still optimal.

The practical takeaway for me is not that we should throw everything out. It's that we should keep running the controlled experiments. Take one component, ask what job it's actually doing, test whether that job still needs doing, and whether something simpler does it. Sometimes the answer is that the component is genuinely essential. Residual connections seem like that. But surprisingly often the answer is that it's a habit.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of truth to it, and a lot of my own work has come from taking that idea seriously. When you look at the components we use today, like normalization layers, specific activation functions, or the way we stack blocks, many of them weren't chosen because someone carefully proved they were necessary. They were chosen because they worked at the time, under particular constraints: certain hardware, certain datasets, a certain training budget, and whatever tricks the community had figured out by then. Once something works and gets into a popular codebase, everyone builds on top of it, and after a few years it starts to feel like a law of nature rather than a design decision.

ConvNeXt was a good example of this for me. The common story around 2020 and 2021 was that Transformers beat ConvNets because attention is fundamentally better for vision. But when we went back and modernized a standard ResNet step by step, borrowing the training recipe, larger kernels, different normalization, fewer activations, and so on, we found that a pure ConvNet could match or exceed a Vision Transformer. So a big part of the gap wasn't the architecture family itself. It was the accumulation of design choices and training practices that had evolved alongside Transformers and never been carried back to ConvNets.

Normalization is another one. LayerNorm and BatchNorm have been treated as essentially indispensable, especially in Transformers. But in our work on Dynamic Tanh, we found you can remove the normalization layers entirely and replace them with a very simple element-wise tanh with a learnable scale, and the models still train well and reach similar performance. That doesn't mean normalization was useless. It solved real optimization problems. But the specific form we settled on was probably one point in a much larger space of solutions, and we just happened to find that one first.

So my view is that we should treat these components with some healthy skepticism. They're not arbitrary. They usually solve a real problem. But the particular solution that became standard is often path-dependent. If the field had developed in a different order, with different hardware or different benchmarks, we might be using quite different building blocks today and calling those the obvious ones. To me that's actually encouraging, because it means there's still a lot of room to simplify and to rethink things we take for granted.

fable-5.text:
That's a framing I find quite sympathetic, actually, because a lot of my own research has been about going back and questioning components that everyone treats as given.

If you look at how architectures actually evolve, it's very path-dependent. A component gets introduced at a particular moment, under particular conditions — a certain scale of data, certain hardware, certain training recipes — and it works, so it gets adopted. Then the field moves on, the conditions change, but the component stays, because nobody wants to touch something that works. Over time it stops being a design decision and becomes a kind of inherited assumption. People don't even ask why it's there anymore.

We saw this with ConvNeXt. When vision transformers came out, the narrative was that attention was the key ingredient. But when we took a standard ConvNet and simply modernized it — the training recipe, the stage ratios, the activation and normalization choices, many of which were borrowed from the transformer era — it matched transformers. So a lot of what looked like an architectural breakthrough was really the surrounding choices, which had accumulated somewhat accidentally.

Normalization layers are another example. Layer norm is in essentially every transformer, and most people would say it's indispensable. But we found you can replace it with something as simple as an element-wise tanh with a learnable scale, and the model trains just as well. That tells you the component survived more because of convention than because it's the unique solution.

That said, I wouldn't say everything is accidental. Some components persist because they genuinely capture something — residual connections are probably in that category. The useful mindset is just to treat every component as a hypothesis rather than a law. Periodically re-derive the architecture from current conditions, and you often find the design space is much larger than the field assumes.

opus-5.text:
I'd soften "accident" a little and say "path-dependent." Most of these components weren't arbitrary — they solved a real problem for someone, with the optimizers, hardware, and data scales of that moment. What happens is that the problem goes away, or gets solved elsewhere, and the component stays. It gets inherited, re-implemented, written into the default config, and after a few years people stop being able to tell the difference between "this is necessary" and "this is what everyone does."

Normalization layers are my favorite example. Batch norm showed up with a story about internal covariate shift, that story didn't really survive scrutiny, and the layer survived anyway — for ten years it was in essentially every serious vision and language model. And when we actually went and replaced it in Transformers with a scaled elementwise tanh, training was fine. That doesn't mean normalization is useless. It means the necessity we'd assigned to it was never established, just assumed.

The same thing happened with ConvNets versus Transformers. A lot of what looked like an architectural verdict was really a difference in training recipes and a handful of design choices. Once you port those over, the gap mostly closes.

So the practical upshot for me isn't iconoclasm for its own sake. It's that in a field moving this fast, the set of things worth re-testing grows faster than anyone re-tests them. The defaults are where the free results are hiding.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of truth in it, though "accident" is a little too strong. A better word is path dependence. A component gets introduced at a particular time, with particular hardware, datasets, and training recipes. It works well enough, everyone builds on top of it, and soon the whole stack, from kernels to libraries to intuitions, is tuned around it. After that, nobody questions it, because it's expensive to question something everything else depends on.

Normalization layers are a good example from my own work. For years people treated them as essentially indispensable in deep networks, and in transformers we all just used LayerNorm without thinking. But when we looked closely at what it was actually doing in trained models, it behaved a lot like a squashing, tanh-like function. We found we could replace it with a very simple element-wise operation and get comparable performance. So a component that seemed fundamental was more replaceable than we assumed.

The ConvNeXt work taught me something similar. A big part of what looked like an architectural advantage of transformers over ConvNets came from training recipes and a handful of macro design choices, not from attention itself.

At the same time, I wouldn't say everything is arbitrary. Components that survive across many scales, tasks, and years of people trying to beat them are probably capturing something real. So I treat these components as hypotheses rather than facts. Ablate them, try simpler alternatives, and keep what actually holds up. Sometimes you'll find the component really matters, and sometimes you'll find it was just inherited.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think a lot of them are, but "accident" can mean two different things. Some components are arbitrary choices that happened to win in a particular era, shaped by the hardware, the datasets, and the training recipes people had at the time. When we modernized a standard ResNet, borrowing training recipes and macro design choices from transformers, much of the gap closed. That suggested a lot of the supposed architectural superiority was really about everything around the convolution, not the convolution itself.

But other components are more like solutions to real problems. Residual connections, for example, keep gradients flowing through deep networks, and it's hard to imagine training very deep models without some version of them. So I'd separate "this was the only way" from "this was the way we found first."

The part I find most interesting is path dependence. Once a component is wired into libraries, optimized kernels, pretrained checkpoints, and people's intuitions, it becomes very sticky, even if something simpler would work just as well. Normalization is a good example. It became almost sacred, but we've found that you can replace it with a fairly simple elementwise function and still train well. That doesn't mean normalization was pointless. It means we confused "useful in the setting where we discovered it" with "essential."

So my view is that we should keep questioning these components, but test them carefully instead of assuming either that they're sacred or that they're arbitrary.

That doesn’t mean the original choice was wrong. It may have been a very good choice at the time. But if the training setup changes, or we have much more data and compute, we should ask whether that component is still helping.

If the network works well, people reuse those choices. Over time, something that was initially just a reasonable decision can start to look like a necessary ingredient.

But calling it a historical accident doesn’t mean it’s a bad design. It means we should be willing to ask whether the original reason still applies. Would we make the same choice today, with a different training setup or a different computational budget?

For me, that’s an experimental question. You change the component, keep the comparison as controlled as possible, and see what happens. Sometimes you discover that it really matters.
